star-ferry.title: The Star Ferry Crosses the Harbour
star-ferry.subtitle: A ferry ride with Grandma
star-ferry.quote: Crossing the harbour is not just a crossing; it is sitting with Grandma for a while.
star-ferry.intro: On Sunday, Grandma takes you to Tsim Sha Tsui to ride the Star Ferry across the harbour. The pier bell rings, and the green ferry comes alongside.

star-1.title: Tsim Sha Tsui Pier
star-1.text: On Sunday, Grandma holds your hand and walks you to the Tsim Sha Tsui pier. The sea breeze tastes a little salty. The bell rings, and the green Star Ferry slowly comes alongside. Grandma taps her Octopus card: “Today we cross the harbour by boat.”

star-2a.title: Sea breeze upstairs
star-2a.text: You and Grandma sit upstairs. The wooden bench is a little cool, and the sea wind messes up your hair. Grandma points to the far shore: “That side is Central, and further along is Wan Chai. When you were small, I took you on this ferry for the first time, and you were still crying.”

star-2b.title: Sounds downstairs
star-2b.text: You sit downstairs. The ferry rocks gently. A sailor throws a thick rope onto the pier and pulls it tight. Grandma teaches you: “Sit still and watch the sea, and you will not feel seasick.”

star-3a.title: Ending · Seven boats
star-3a.text: You lean on the railing and count the boats: one, two, three… By the seventh, the ferry has already reached the pier. Grandma laughs: “That is enough. Count any more and you will not want to leave.”
star-3a.endingText: Some views only come clear when you sit down and look slowly.

star-3b.title: Ending · Grandma's listener
star-3b.text: You lean close to Grandma's ear: “When I grow up, I want to learn to tell stories like you.” Grandma pauses, then smiles so widely her eyes almost disappear: “Good. Next time you tell one, and I will listen.” The ferry reaches the pier, and the bell rings again.
star-3b.endingText: Crossing the harbour is not just a crossing; it is sitting with Grandma for a while.

star-1: Sit upstairs and watch the view
Sit downstairs and listen to the ferry

过海.note: Hong Kong people call a ferry crossing “crossing the sea”.

嘟一嘟.note: The Octopus is Hong Kong's common transit card.

喊.note: In Cantonese, “haam” means to cry, not to shout.

水手.note: On the Star Ferry, sailors throw the mooring rope when docking.

栏杆.note: Hold the railing when you look at the sea.

靠岸.note: Once the ferry has docked, passengers can get off.

讲故.note: Hong Kong people say “gong gu” for storytelling.

见牙唔见眼.meaning: Smile so widely that your eyes disappear
见牙唔见眼.note: A playful way to say someone is grinning from ear to ear.

tram-token.title: The Old Tram Ticket
tram-token.subtitle: Grandpa and an old tram ticket
tram-token.quote: One ding-ding, and the whole street slows down.
tram-token.intro: Grandpa is tidying a drawer when he finds an old tram ticket. He takes you from Kennedy Town to Causeway Bay on the ding-ding and promises a story about a tram conductor.

tram-1.title: Kennedy Town Terminus
tram-1.text: Grandpa tidies a drawer and finds a yellowed tram ticket. He says: “Today I will take you on the ding-ding, from Kennedy Town all the way to Causeway Bay.” At the terminus, a green tram goes ding-ding and slowly pulls in.

tram-2a.title: Front-row seat
tram-2a.text: You sit in the front row. The driver presses a foot pedal, the bell goes ding-ding, and the whole street seems to slow down. Grandpa says: “When I was young, the tram still had a rope you pulled to stop.”

tram-2b.title: Window seat upstairs
tram-2b.text: You and Grandpa sit by the upstairs window. The tram passes North Point, where the market entrance is crowded and umbrellas are packed shoulder to shoulder. Grandpa looks out: “I used to be a conductor on this very line.”

tram-3a.title: Ending · Why ding-ding
tram-3a.text: Grandpa says: “The tram rings ding-ding before a stop to warn people to step aside. Before Octopus cards, the conductor collected every fare and remembered who had not paid.” The tram reaches Causeway Bay, and Grandpa puts the old ticket back in your palm.
tram-3a.endingText: Tickets grow old, but the ding-ding sounds the same.

tram-3b.title: Ending · His first day at work
tram-3b.text: The tram reaches Causeway Bay, and Grandpa leads you off. You look back as the ding-ding rings again, carrying a car full of people slowly away. Grandpa says: “One old ticket holds the whole afternoon of my first day at work.”
tram-3b.endingText: One old ticket holds a whole afternoon.

tram-2a: Ask Grandpa why it is called ding-ding
Help Grandpa watch for our stop
tram-2b: Ask Grandpa why it is called ding-ding
Help Grandpa watch for our stop

叮叮.note: The tram rings “ding-ding” at stops, so people call it the ding-ding.

埋站.note: Used for buses and trams arriving at a stop.

车头.note: The front row gives the clearest view ahead.

后生.note: “Hau saang” refers to youth and prime years.

遮.note: Hong Kong people call an umbrella a “je”.

车长.note: Old tram conductors pulled a rope to signal the driver.

八达通.note: Hong Kong's all-purpose transit and payment card.

手心.note: Elders often place small things in a child's palm.

落车.note: Cantonese says “get down from the vehicle”.

返工.note: Going to work is “fan gung”; finishing work is “sau gung”.

cha-chaan-teng.title: Pineapple Bun at the Cha Chaan Teng
cha-chaan-teng.subtitle: A glass of iced lemon tea on a rainy day
cha-chaan-teng.quote: One “m goi”, and the whole cha chaan teng feels warmer.
cha-chaan-teng.intro: On a rainy day, Mum takes you into a cha chaan teng to shelter from the rain. The waiter hands over a menu, but you only see the pineapple bun at the next table.
cha-chaan-teng.dialect: Cantonese · Hong Kong cha chaan teng

cha-1.title: A rainy day at the cha chaan teng
cha-1.text: It is raining, and Mum pulls you into a cha chaan teng to shelter. The waiter calls out loudly: “Sit anywhere!” You see the pineapple bun at the next table, butter slowly melting into the warm bread. Mum teaches you: “When you want something, say ‘m goi’.”

cha-2a.title: Ordering by yourself
cha-2a.text: You raise your hand and say quietly: “M goi, one pineapple bun, one iced lemon tea, less sweet.” The waiter repeats it with a smile and even winks at you: “Clever one!”

cha-2b.title: Learning to order
cha-2b.text: Mum orders for you: “One pineapple bun, one iced lemon tea, less sweet.” You repeat after her, phrase by phrase, and the waiter nods: “This kid is good.”

cha-3a.title: Ending · Half each
cha-3a.text: The pineapple bun arrives. Hot bread holds a slab of cold butter, melting bit by bit. Mum cuts it in half: one half for you, one for her. Outside the rain keeps falling, and the table feels warm.
cha-3a.endingText: The best pineapple bun is the one shared with Mum.

cha-3b.title: Ending · One big thank you
cha-3b.text: You walk to the counter and tell the waiter: “M goi saai!” He grins from ear to ear and gives you a small egg tart. Mum says: “One thank-you, and the whole shop is happy.”
cha-3b.endingText: One “m goi”, and the whole cha chaan teng feels warmer.

cha-1: Ask Mum to order for you

茶餐厅.note: A casual cafe serving milk tea, pineapple buns, and rice dishes.

唔该.note: One of Hong Kong's most common polite phrases.

落单.note: Hong Kong people say “lok daan” for ordering food.

少甜.note: Common when ordering iced lemon tea; “no sugar” is “zau tim”.

冻柠茶.note: A cha chaan teng classic; you usually muddle the lemon yourself.

上枱.note: Food being brought to the table is “seung toi”.

唔该晒.note: Adding “saai” to “m goi” makes the thanks stronger.

蛋挞.note: A favourite fresh from the oven at cha chaan tengs and bakeries.
